doc.title: John LaPorta interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

chapter: Early bands and the swing era
title: Why the big bands ended and how times change
summary: LaPorta discusses swing as dance music, the postwar economics and television behind the big band collapse in 1946, and how each generation hears its own music.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: So at this time, we sometimes have a hard time getting the picture that jazz was really the popular music of the day, or swing oriented.

Well my feeling about that is that essentially the music was all in danceable tempos you know, the swing and the sweet bands and everything else, they were all playing pretty much the same kinds of tempos that people could relate to them and dance to them. As jazz started to become more of an art form, it got into, by the very process of evolution, got into doing different kinds of things, getting into different kinds of time signatures and variations and things like that. and then the music got more complex too so there became a division there. That’s probably an over simplification, I’m sure it’s more complex than that.
Yeah, but when it got into the bop period for instance, it became a lot of times much quicker tempos and less danceable.

I think there was economic considerations that went on. There weren’t, for a long time there weren’t records. People had to go. Sometimes they drove a hundred, a hundred fifty miles to go see a band you know. So this had a lot to do with the live aspect of performance in that time. But when Woody’s band broke up in late ‘46, records were becoming quite commonplace. The bands were becoming very expensive to field, the economy was not good then, and there was a whole combination of elements. Woody’s band was doing very well. He broke up for other reasons. He had family problems and he had to get back and mend some fences, but found that after a year he couldn’t tolerate not being with a band, and went back again. But at that point four or five bands broke up, you

know, the Dorsey Brothers and quite a few of the bands broke up. It was really the end of an era. And television had a great deal to do with it, so there was a whole bunch of factors, I mean as I see it, that came into play then.

It’s interesting because musicians today complain about the same kinds of things almost. They say that the DJs take over some of the work these days, so I guess some things don’t change it’s just the different circumstances. At that time it was the economy, nowadays it’s technology and it’s different things that affect the music, but somehow it goes on.

The times change. People don’t. The characteristics that people have, you know the competitiveness and the things that go into play for things to happen. But music answers different needs at different times you know. I know a lot of the older musicians feel like well, this is, the music now is not any good, of course most of those people, and I’m probably a product of that too, go down memory lane, and they associate the music that was part of their roots and part of their beginnings, so the young people have their own voice in terms of what seems to satisfy them, and the music that is produced is created for the things that seem to be happening with the younger people.
